record.paper_title: Some Open Problems in Matrix Theory Arising in Linear Systems and Control
record.context_brief: transpose-related exponential identities for nonnormal matrices
record.original_question: Does there exist a nonnormal matrix A such that either exp(A) exp(A^T) = exp(A^T) exp(A) or exp(A) exp(A^T) = exp(A + A^T)? The question asks whether a nonnormal real matrix can satisfy either of these exponential identities involving its transpose.

evidence.quote: Specializing to the case A = A^T, a related open question is the following [14]: Does there exist a nonnormal matrix A satisfying either e^A e^{A^T} = e^{A^T} e^A or e^A e^{A^T} = e^{A+A^T}?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ denote the set of $n \times n$ real matrices, and write $A^T$ for the transpose of $A$. The matrix exponential is defined by $\exp(A) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} A^k / k!$. A matrix $A \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is called normal if $A A^T = A^T A$.

Determine whether there exists a nonnormal matrix $A \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ (for some $n \geq 2$) satisfying at least one of the following identities:

(a) $\exp(A)\,\exp(A^T) = \exp(A^T)\,\exp(A)$;

(b) $\exp(A)\,\exp(A^T) = \exp(A + A^T)$.

That is, exhibit such a nonnormal $A$, or prove that for each of (a) and (b) the identity forces $A$ to be normal.
artifact.status_search_result: Hongguo Xu (Linear Algebra Appl., 1997, "Two results about the matrix exponential") addresses both identities. For (b), it is established that $\exp(A)\exp(A^*) = \exp(A+A^*)$ holds if and only if $A$ is normal, so no nonnormal example exists. For (a), Xu gives a characterization of matrices satisfying $\exp(A)\exp(A^*) = \exp(A^*)\exp(A)$, which admits nonnormal solutions. Thus the question is resolved.

status_evidence.title: Two results about the matrix exponential — ScienceDirect
status_evidence.snippet: One characterizes the matrices A which satisfy e^A e^{A^H} = e^{A^H} e^A; another gives upper bounds on trace(e^A e^{A^H}). It is noted that e^A e^{A^H} = e^{A+A^H} if and only if A is normal.
status_evidence.claim: Identity (b) forces normality, while identity (a) admits a characterization including nonnormal matrices.
